nameStory: The 'Hairy Shadow Lichen' gets its name from the tiny, hair-like structures called cilia that fringe its edges, giving it a fuzzy appearance. The 'shadow' part refers to how these lichens often grow in the partial shade of tree bark and rocks, creating subtle gray patterns that blend into the shadows.
description: Hairy Shadow Lichen is a crusty, flat lichen that forms small rosettes or patches on tree bark and rocks. It appears grayish to brownish-gray with a somewhat powdery or granular surface texture. Individual patches typically grow 1-3 inches across, though they can merge to cover larger areas. Like all lichens, it's actually two organisms living together - a fungus and an algae - creating what looks like a single crusty growth.

idTips.label: Hair-like edge fringe
idTips.description: Look closely at the edges with a hand lens - you'll see tiny hair-like projections (cilia) that feel slightly rough to the touch and give the margins a fuzzy appearance

idTips.label: Rosette growth pattern
idTips.description: Forms circular or semi-circular patches that radiate outward from the center, like flower petals arranged in a rosette

idTips.label: Granular surface texture
idTips.description: The surface feels slightly gritty or powdery when gently touched, with a matte finish rather than glossy or smooth

idTips.label: Gray-brown coloration
idTips.description: Ranges from pale gray to brownish-gray, often appearing darker when wet and lighter when dry

idTips.label: Bark preference
idTips.description: Most commonly found on tree bark, especially on the sides of trunks that receive indirect light

habitat: Look for Hairy Shadow Lichen on the bark of deciduous and coniferous trees throughout New England's forests, from sea level to moderate elevations. It prefers spots with partial shade and good air circulation, often on the north or east sides of tree trunks. You might also find it on wooden fence posts or weathered rock surfaces in wooded areas.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more visible as it absorbs moisture from spring rains, appearing darker and more defined against tree bark. This is a good time to spot the hair-like edge features.
seasonality.summer: May appear paler and more powdery during dry spells, but remains identifiable. The rosette patterns are most distinct during stable summer weather.
seasonality.fall: Often at its most photogenic as autumn moisture enhances its coloration and the hair-like margins become more pronounced against the changing bark colors.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round but may appear more muted. Snow and ice can make it harder to spot, but it's still actively growing during mild winter days.

funFact: **[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** This lichen can actually survive being completely frozen and thawed repeatedly throughout winter, essentially going into suspended animation and resuming photosynthesis the moment conditions improve - making it tougher than most plants in New England's harsh climate.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other shadow lichens in the same genus, but the hairy edge fringe is the key distinguishing feature. Memory trick: 'Hairy edges = Hairy Shadow' - if you don't see those tiny hair-like projections around the edges, you're looking at a different species.
compareHints: Among its relatives, Hairy Shadow Lichen is distinguished by those characteristic hair-like edge projections that other shadow lichens lack. **[UNCERTAIN]** The Ciliate Wreath Lichen also has edge hairs but tends to form more distinct, separated rosettes, while Hairy Shadow Lichen often has more irregular, merging patches. Most other shadow lichens in the genus have smooth or slightly wavy edges without the fuzzy fringe.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Phaeophyscia relatives, Orange-cored Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its bright orange pycnidial contents - most other wreath lichens in this genus have white, yellow, or red cores instead.
Among the shadow lichens in its genus, Pom-pom Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its small size and abundant powdery soredia clusters.
Among its wreath lichen relatives, Powder-tipped Shadow Lichen is distinguished by having the white soredia concentrated specifically at the lobe tips rather than scattered across the surface.
Unlike its relatives in the Phaeophyscia genus, Ciliate Wreath Lichen is the only one with prominent white hair-like projections along all lobe edges.
Unlike its relatives in the Phaeophyscia genus, Dark Shadow Lichen is easily recognized by its abundant black isidia that cover both the center and edges of the lobes.

Unlike its relatives such as Orange-cored Shadow Lichen (which has orange inner tissues) or Hairy Shadow Lichen (which has fuzzy edges), Mealy Shadow Lichen lacks both colorful internal tissues and hairy margins.

Unlike its relatives like Orange-cored Shadow Lichen (which has orange interiors) or Mealy Shadow Lichen (which has white powdery surfaces), Red-cored Starburst Shadow Lichen is the only species in its genus with the distinctive crimson interior.
Among its Phaeophyscia relatives, Whiskered Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its particularly prominent marginal cilia and small size.
Among its shadow lichen relatives, Scaly Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its prominently curled, squarrose lobes that create a three-dimensional texture.
